conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you were able to come in today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers like you.  

Over the next few minutes we’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team; my only goal is to keep you safe and feeling heard.  

We’ll walk through ten questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories—and you can answer in your own words. If anything feels difficult, we can pause or come back to it. Ready to begin?  

Here’s the first question:  
In the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even that felt kind of flat or distant?

[soft sigh, eyes down]  
Honestly, most things feel… flat. I still manage to smile when the baby grips my finger, but even that little burst fades fast. Before, a warm cup of coffee or a show I liked could lift me—now they feel kind of “meh.” I can scrape up a flicker of pleasure, but it’s way less than it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile fades quickly]  
Not really… I’ll see something on my phone that used to make me giggle, and I might sort of chuckle, but it’s like the laugh dies before it fully comes out. Nothing feels truly funny anymore—just tired and kind of gray.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet voice, fingers twisting in lap]  
Barely. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, even a walk. This week, when I think about anything coming up, I just feel... empty, like, “what’s the point?” I still go through the motions, but there’s no real spark of looking forward to it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up, voice shaky]  
Yeah... I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or that I'm just not soothing him right. My partner says I'm doing fine, but in my head it's always "I'm failing as a mom." Even little things—like dropping a burp cloth—I'll replay it and tell myself I'm useless.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, rubbing thumb against palm]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll just be sitting there, baby finally asleep, and suddenly my chest feels tight—like something awful is about to happen. I check his breathing over and over, or worry the ceiling fan will fall on him. There’s no real reason, but I can’t turn the fear off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
Yeah... a couple times this week. I'll be rocking the baby in the chair and out of nowhere my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, like I need to run out of the room. There's nothing actually wrong, but in that moment I'm sure something terrible is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]  
Yes... most days. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, laundry's everywhere, and I just freeze. I feel like I'm drowning in small tasks. Sometimes I sit on the floor and cry because I can't figure out which thing to do first. My partner tells me to rest, but even resting feels like one more thing I'm failing at.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[wrings the hem of my sweater]  
Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—did I sterilize the bottles, is the baby breathing, why did I say that dumb thing to my mom? It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound. I’m lucky if I get three broken hours before he needs me again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods, voice small]  
Most of the week. It’s like a heavy blanket that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tearful for no reason, or I catch myself staring at the wall feeling hollow inside. It’s not every single moment—sometimes I’ll feel okay for a bit—but the sadness keeps sliding back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quiet, eyes fixed on the floor]  
Yeah... maybe twice in the past week. Last night I sat in the nursery after finally getting him down, and it just hit me—this wave of sadness. I cried into a burp cloth so I wouldn't wake anyone. It felt like the tears came from nowhere and everywhere at once.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice drops to a whisper]  
Once or twice... just fleeting. Like, "what if I just kept driving past the grocery store and didn’t come back?" I’d never do anything—I love my baby—but the picture flashed for a second. No plan, no real wish to die... just this quick, scary thought that I’m failing and everyone might be better off without me. It scares me that it even pops in.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly gray-joy is fleeting, laughter fades before it begins, and even small tasks feel like drowning. Despite loving your baby, you're carrying relentless worry, sudden panic, tearful spells, and haunting thoughts that everyone might be better off without you. These feelings are not your fault, and you deserve help lifting that heavy blanket.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports total loss of ability to enjoy humor, describing laughter that dies immediately and feeling gray, matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, describing feelings of emptiness and lack of spark, aligning with 'Hardly at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses pervasive self-blame, linking even minor mishaps to personal failure as a mother</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, distressing anxiety without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden intense panic episodes with racing heart, urge to flee, and dread without trigger, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days," describes being paralyzed by daily tasks, crying from inability to prioritize, and perceiving rest as failure—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, prolonged sleep onset (>1h), frequent awakenings, and total sleep ≤3h, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness most of the week, tearfulness, and persistent low mood—clearly matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: persistent low mood and loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) most of the day, nearly every day; <sym>insomnia</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, diminished concentration, and recurrent passive <sym>suicidal ideation</sym>. With a score ≥14 and Q10 ≥1, urgent referral is indicated per EPDS guidelines. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with <med>obstetric mental-health team</med> or <med>psychiatry</med> for full diagnostic evaluation and safety planning
2. Mobilize trusted support person to stay with you until professional review; share crisis contacts
3. Call 988 (US) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify
4. Begin basic sleep-hygiene strategies: 15-min wind-down, low light, delegate one night feed if possible
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
6. Provide educational materials on <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med> to normalize recovery
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, first live birth, partner supportive, bottle-feeding.

Symptoms endorsed (all 10 EPDS items):
1. Persistent low mood, anhedonia (laugh dies, “gray,” no spark)  
2. Marked guilt / self-blame (“I’m failing as a mom,” ruminates over trivial incidents)  
3. Daily free-floating anxiety, catastrophic worries (baby safety, ceiling fan)  
4. Panic symptoms: sudden tachycardia, urge to flee, resolves in minutes  
5. Overwhelm / paralysis by routine tasks (“drowning,” floor-crying)  
6. Initial and maintenance insomnia related to racing worries  
7. Frequent crying spells, sadness “slides back in”  
8. Fleeting passive suicidal ideation (“keep driving, everyone better off”) without plan or intent

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for ≥2 wk; interfere with caretaking, sleep, and functioning.

Risk flags  
– Depressed mood + anhedonia + guilt → high likelihood of major depressive episode  
– Anxiety/panic symptoms meet criteria for co-occurring anxiety disorder  
– Passive SI present → safety concern; requires same-day risk assessment and safety-planning  
– No psychosis, no manic symptoms, no substance use endorsed

Screening impression: High-risk for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; safety evaluation indicated.

Next steps: Recommend immediate referral to OB mental-health team / psychiatry for full diagnostic interview, SI assessment, and treatment planning; confirm support person at home; provide crisis resources.
